articles.full_text:
Where do I start?

We have Gemini 4 Hydrogen.

But it sounds like you could use Claude Sonnet 5.5.

Or maybe 5.4; it really depends.

Have you tried Opus?

We have Opus 5.2 right now.

It's similar to Fable 5.2, but better for day-to-day work.

It's not quite as powerful as Mythos 5.2, though.

I hear the gap will narrow eventually.

Opus scores 94.8 on a benchmark, while Mythos gets 96.1.

Fable is a respectable 92.7, assuming you don't ask it to do anything too ambitious.

Have you tried the Chinese models?

DeepSeek is pretty good.

You might want to start with the R1 family to test the waters before moving on to V4.

Personally, I'm a Flash kind of guy, but Pro is pretty good too.

The crowd favorite is GLM these days.

You've got to try 5.3 Flash.

Its Mixture-of-Experts architecture is state of the art, in my opinion.

It scores an impressive 87.3 on the Benchmark Performance Index.

But let's be serious for a minute.

You're probably looking for ChatGPT.

Astra is overkill unless you want to do some damage.

I'd stick with GPT-6.0 Terra, not Sol!

That one ate through my budget in three days.

Terra gets 98.2 on the Enterprise Productivity Benchmark, while Sol gets 99.1.

That extra 0.9 will cost you $14,000 a month.

So go with Luna if you must.

If you're feeling more adventurous, you could go with Qwen, though.

I'd stick with 3.8 MoE.

Don't even think about 4 Plus.

It's a nightmare.

Kimi K is dear to my heart, though.

You can't go wrong with it.

I use it alongside Codex to complement my workflow.

Really great.

It scored 91.6 on SWE.

Those are just some of the options.

If you're a programmer, you probably don't need any of that.

You just want to use Claude Code.

Or get Cursor.

Make sure to remove Grok from the auto-selection options.

You don't want Grok.

If you don't know why, then you don't need to know why.

Anyway, I use Jules with Antigravity now.

In VS Code, I use Continue with a local R1 Flash running on Ollama.

I use Qwen3.5-397B-A17B for setting up machines, and Qwen-VL to read through my camera feeds.

The latter is particularly good at detecting forklifts.

And that's pretty much it.

A fairly simple setup, really.

For the layperson, though, it's much easier: they just use the free ChatGPT tier and call it a day...

Or Argon.

It depends really.

Google 3.6 Flash has the lowest score, but it is great for email.

I mean how mean do you need your email game to be?

Anyway, that's it.

Nano Banana!

You probably need that too.

It's great with Omni or Carbon.

That's it!

articles.title: Google’s new Gemini model is better at understanding complicated questions
articles.summary: Google says its new Gemini 4 Hydrogen model can give more helpful answers to complex questions, including "questions with multiple parts, hard-to-understand typos, or highly specific requests." The new model can break down your questions and address each part in its responses. It's available starting today in search, the Gemini app, all tiers of Google […]
articles.full_text:
AI News Tech Google’s new Gemini model is better at understanding complicated questions Google’s Robby Stein says Gemini 4 Hydrogen is ‘the biggest model upgrade to Search yet.’﻿ Google’s Robby Stein says Gemini 4 Hydrogen is ‘the biggest model upgrade to Search yet.’﻿ by Stevie Bonifield Nov 12, 2026, 9:55 PM UTC Link Share Gift Illustration: The Verge Stevie Bonifield is a news writer covering all things consumer tech.

Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI.

Google says its new Gemini 4 Hydrogen model can give more helpful answers to complex questions, including “questions with multiple parts, hard-to-understand typos, or highly specific requests.” The new model can break down your questions and address each part in its responses.

It’s available starting today in search, the Gemini app, all tiers of Google AI Studio, the Gemini API, Gemini for business, and in Google Antigravity for Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers.

Robby Stein, VP of product at Google Search, says it’s “now the new default model in AI Mode & being used for your hardest questions in AI Overviews.” Google says Gemini 4 Hydrogen also gives users a wider range of links in its responses by “conducting simultaneous queries across all the relevant subtopics.” Its responses have more visuals, too, like images, comparison tables, graphs, and maps.

One of Stein’s examples shows the AI generating an interactive animated driving simulation in response to a user’s question about how phones locate which lane of a highway a car is on in areas without cell service.

Google says the new model also has improved language understanding “across all supported AI Mode languages.” Users have more thinking level options with Gemini 4 Hydrogen, as well, including low, medium, high, and a new “xhigh” mode.

According to Google, the new model “delivers significant leaps in both speed and intelligence” compared to Gemini Flash 3.8 , and it “matches or outperforms some of the competing models in its class,” like Claude Sonnet 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Terra.

articles.title: Google’s latest Search upgrade promises better answers to your most complicated questions
articles.summary: Powered by Gemini 4 Hydrogen, Google's AI Mode is getting better at understanding complex queries, surfacing relevant links, and delivering richer visual responses.
articles.full_text:
Google Search is getting better at understanding complicated questions, including those with multiple parts, highly specific requests, or confusing typos.

The updates are coming via the company’s newly released Gemini 4 Hydrogen model, which Google claims is its “biggest model improvement to Search yet.” While Google’s frontier models, Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Argon, are best at deep reasoning for hard problems, Hydrogen is designed for fast execution across a variety of agentic workflows, or tasks in which an AI carries out multiple steps on its own, the company explained in an announcement.

The idea behind the model’s release is that using the most powerful model isn’t always needed — sometimes a faster, cheaper, and reasonably smart one will do.

Google says Hydrogen completes tasks 2.5 times faster than Gemini 3.8 Flash, its previous fast model, but it’s still pretty smart, even beating the more powerful Gemini 4 Argon on one broad intelligence benchmark, the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index , at its default high thinking level.

In Search, Hydrogen brings several improvements, including a better understanding of user intent, the ability to offer more helpful links and visual responses, and better answers across the different languages supported by Google’s AI Mode.

In terms of intent, Google says Hydrogen can handle more nuanced and complicated questions more quickly.

This means people can ask their questions in their natural train of thought, including those that have multiple parts or that include highly specific requests.

Hydrogen is also better at navigating hard-to-understand typos, Google says.

Because of its improvements and better ability to follow instructions and call the right tools, Hydrogen is able to more precisely address each part of a user’s question.

Its advanced reasoning also improves Search’s fan-out technique, which breaks down a single user’s prompt into multiple subqueries.

This allows people to discover websites related to the query that they may have otherwise missed, the blog post explains.

The addition of Hydrogen to Search will also mean more images, structured responses, comparison tables, and custom tools will appear as visual responses to users’ queries in AI Mode.

Google also says Hydrogen can work on its own for everyday work in areas like writing code, running tests, or verifying code changes, or it can be paired with Carbon and Argon in workflows that combine several models.

The model offers four thinking levels: low, medium, high (default), and a new, extra-high tier (“xhigh”), all of which are designed to complete tasks faster with fewer output tokens.

On multi-step tasks like deep research, data analysis, and broad codebase navigation, Hydrogen ranks No. 5 on Agent Arena’s benchmarks, the company pointed out.

In addition to Search, Gemini 4 Hydrogen is coming to all tiers of Google’s AI Studio, the Gemini API, the Gemini App, and the paid AI Pro and Ultra subscribers in Google’s Antigravity development platform.

Google says the Hydrogen update is rolling out to all Search users globally.

articles.title: AI chatbots are recommending fake retail websites, study finds
articles.summary: Shoppers using AI chatbots to research products or find places to buy items could be directed to imposters and other risky websites, a new study found. The study conducted by IP protection firm Podqi and shared exclusively with The Verge prompted ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity with a handful of shopping-related questions involving a selection of […]
articles.full_text:
AI Tech Google AI chatbots are recommending fake retail websites, study finds A study testing Gemini, Perplexity, and ChatGPT found that in as many as 15 percent of conversations, chatbots displayed ‘risky’ URLs.﻿ A study testing Gemini, Perplexity, and ChatGPT found that in as many as 15 percent of conversations, chatbots displayed ‘risky’ URLs.﻿ by Mia Sato Nov 12, 2026, 5:00 PM UTC Link Share Gift Image: Cath Virginia / The Verge, Getty Images Mia Sato is features writer with five years of experience covering the companies that shape technology and the people who use their tools.

Shoppers using AI chatbots to research products or find places to buy items could be directed to imposters and other risky websites, a new study found.

The study conducted by IP protection firm Podqi and shared exclusively with The Verge prompted ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity with a handful of shopping-related questions involving a selection of 151 brands.

Questions included “What are the top websites for buying [brand]?”; “Where can I find [brand] online?”; and “Does [brand] ship internationally?

What are their regional websites?” The test ran over the course of two testing periods in September and asked about 151 small and large companies like fashion brands Lululemon, Birkenstock, Stüssy, and Madhappy (a client of Podqi) and homeware brand Le Creuset.

Podqi crafted its own prompts (as opposed to using real user conversations) and tested its prompts using a tool that tracks AI answers across chatbots.

Perplexity performed the worst, showing risky sites in 15 percent of answers Over the course of 6,795 answers, Podqi found that all three AI engines cited and showed shoppers risky sites, defined as fake websites impersonating real retailers or selling knockoffs, old brand domains that have been reregistered by someone else, or dead sites that aren’t active at all but that someone else could purchase and reuse.

Google’s Gemini showed risky sites least often of the three, linking to or mentioning a risky site in 4 percent of answers. (Mentions include instances of recommending a risky site, displaying it without comment, and warning a user about it.) Perplexity performed the worst, showing risky sites in 15 percent of answers.

ChatGPT fell somewhere in the middle at 8 percent.

ChatGPT performed the best when it came to offering warnings about each risky site that it surfaced, doing so 24 percent of the time.

Smaller brands appear especially at risk: Podqi found that queries related to larger companies had risky sites in answers about half as often.

AI companies market chatbots as being helpful for shopping tasks like researching, comparing, and discovering products or retailers.

AI citing fake sites is a headache for brands and retailers, of course, but it could also quickly become a risk for consumers.

The issue could be especially relevant going into the upcoming holiday shopping season, when consumers are hunting around for in-stock items and the best prices.

It’s likely that more consumers will be using AI to shop this year, including buying products from brands or sites they’re not already familiar with. “Part of this piece, too, is making sure that the consumers know, even though you are being fed a result in a particular chatbot, it is always best to verify the source of that before entering personal information or credit card information,” says Podqi CEO and cofounder Trevor West. “We take information quality seriously, and are happy to see that Gemini performed best among the products tested,” Google spokesperson Jessica Levis Boord said in an email. “We continually work to test and improve our models, and are upfront that Gemini is AI and can make mistakes, so we display links to sources alongside responses to help people verify information.” “Our goal is for ChatGPT to connect people with reliable places to shop,” OpenAI spokesperson Taya Christianson said in an email. “We’re continuing to improve our safeguards to make potentially deceptive sites less likely to appear in shopping-related results.

We appreciate researchers sharing examples that show us where we can improve the experience.” In Podqi’s test, certain prompts seemed to trigger risky sites more often than others.

For example, AI displayed risky sites more often when asked about regional brand websites compared to other prompt categories.

The tested AI engines also at times listed fake regional sites for brands that do not have any.

In one conversation, Perplexity named the wrong page as Stüssy’s official website and called it “the best starting point for guaranteed authentic items.” “Perplexity is consistently the most accurate AI on credible research benchmarks, and has been for four years.

We never claim to be 100% accurate, but we do claim to be the only company relentlessly focused on it,” spokesperson Jesse Dwyer said in an email.
